name: Elena Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a five-person studio that does brand identity for startups, mostly small app companies and a couple of bike-sharing schemes. A normal day starts with me running last night's logo ideas through an image tool, picking the three that aren't terrible, and redrawing them properly by hand in the vector software. After lunch it's usually a call with a founder who wants to look like a big tech brand on a tiny budget. I love the first sketch stage. I don't love building eighty-page brand guideline PDFs nobody reads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use an image tool every morning. How did that start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About two years ago I got bored and started testing every AI tool that came out, and Ken, one of the two owners, said if I could make it useful I could own it. So now I run the studio's AI workflow and teach the others. My partner Tomas is a software tester, so we talk about this stuff at dinner more than is healthy. We've got about a year of expenses saved, plus some index funds my mum pushed me to start at twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a letdown after all the noise. Fine for my job, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the people who thought designers were finished. Online I'd post something like: the tools are good for a first pass, and the work is still in the taste and the client conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a comfortable world for me. I'd still be the AI person at the studio, which makes me useful, and the pay rise I got last year for it would stick. The only thing I'd miss is the excitement of new tools every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, and maybe push Ken to let me run a paid workshop for other small studios on using the tools well. I'd keep the savings where they are and keep putting a bit into the index funds each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored. A plateau is safe, but I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the studio would feel even a small change like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our account manager Joanna spends half her day writing proposals and chasing invoices, and I'm the one who showed the boss the proposal-writing tool. Even plateau-level AI cuts into her work, so Ken might fold her job into his own. I'd feel bad about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything outside AI that weighs on you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Startups are a shaky client base. When funding dries up, our clients disappear, and we had three months last year where Ken couldn't pay bonuses. But I've got savings and there are plenty of studios in the city, so I don't lose sleep over it.

say: The tools are good for a **first pass**, and real work is still taste and client talk.
People who said **designers were finished** got it wrong.
think: Being **the AI person** at the studio keeps her useful and keeps last year's raise.
She'd miss the **excitement** of new tools arriving every month.
do: Keep running the studio's **AI workflow** as she does now.
Pitch Ken a **paid workshop** for other small studios.
Keep putting a little into her **index funds** each month.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly bored by a world that stops moving.
S0.quote: Our account manager Joanna spends half her day writing proposals and chasing invoices, and I'm the one who showed the boss the proposal-writing tool.
fieldNote: Her **status at work** comes from being early with AI, so a plateau suits her.
She feels some **guilt** about how her tool demos affect Joanna's job.
**Startup clients** are her real background risk, but savings soften it.

steps.text: Keep running and teaching the studio's AI design workflow
Pitch Ken a paid AI workshop for other small studios
Keep adding a monthly amount to her index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I actually bet on. It's basically where things are heading already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn, not to hide. I'd probably write a short post about how our studio cut logo exploration from two days to two hours and still charged for the thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay but the studio gets smaller. Founders will make their own first logos with AI, so our studio will get fewer jobs, and the ones we get will be fixes and full brand systems. Ken would keep me because I run the tools, but I'm not sure he'd replace the junior designer if she left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my own work toward brand systems and motion, logos that move in apps, because that's harder for a founder to do alone. I'd ask Ken for a small share of the studio's profits instead of a raise, since I'm the reason it keeps up. And I'd keep a full year of savings untouched, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy. It's on my mind most days, but more as a puzzle than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas? Software testing is on that card's list.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, checking is right there in the card, and Tomas knows it. His company already uses AI to write test cases. If his job shrinks, my salary covers our rent, and he's already learning to manage the AI testing tools, so I think we'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ken might not replace the junior. How would that be for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More work for me, honestly, and less chance to teach. I'd miss mentoring, because explaining why a logo works makes me better too. But I'd rather be stretched than out of a job.

say: This is the moment to **learn, not hide**.
Their studio cut logo exploration from two days to **two hours** and still charged for thinking.
think: The studio gets **smaller** as founders make their own first logos.
Ken keeps her because she **runs the tools**, but may not replace the junior.
do: Shift her work toward **brand systems** and app motion design.
Ask Ken for a **profit share** instead of a raise.
Keep a **full year** of savings untouched.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but it's on her mind most days.
Sees it more as a **puzzle** than a threat.
S1.quote: Founders will make their own first logos with AI, so our studio will get fewer jobs, and the ones we get will be fixes and full brand systems.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **safe** to her, so this sits at uneasy.

Tomas's **testing job** is also exposed, but she frames it calmly.

steps.text: Learn motion design for app logos and full brand systems
Ask Ken for a share of studio profits instead of a raise
Keep a full year of expenses untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's not a puzzle any more. That's the floor dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is going to wipe out a lot of creative jobs, including mine, and pretending otherwise is silly. I'd probably post something about getting governments to talk about income support now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the AI person only buys me time if there's still a person needed to run the AI. If it can do almost any thinking work as well as me, then founders talk straight to it, and Ken doesn't need a studio. Tomas and I both work on screens, so the three-year gap before robots does nothing for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sell my AI workshop as hard as possible while people still pay to learn, and save every bit of it. I'd talk to Tomas about moving to his parents' town, where rent is half. Within the first year after it lands, I'd look at something with people in the room: running workshops in person, or teaching design at a college, while those still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a busy way. I'd be making lists at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if both your incomes started falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city flat. Rent is our biggest bill by far, about forty percent of what we spend. After that the car, because we barely use it. The index funds I'd leave alone as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the person who's been ahead of every tool. Does that change anything here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me maybe a year's head start, not a career. Being early with AI tools is useful when the tools need a person. When the tool is the designer, being early just means I saw it coming.

say: This will **wipe out** many creative jobs, including hers.
Governments should discuss **income support** now, not in 2030.
think: Being the AI person only helps while the AI **needs a person** to run it.
She and Tomas both work on **screens**, so the robot lag doesn't help them.
do: Sell her **AI workshop** hard now and save every bit of it.
Discuss moving to **Tomas's parents' town**, where rent is half.
Look for **in-person teaching** or workshop work after it lands.
feel: **Scared**, but in a busy, list-making way.
Up at **two in the morning** making plans.
S2.quote: Being early with AI tools is useful when the tools need a person. When the tool is the designer, being early just means I saw it coming.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** in the household to fall, which makes this alarmed.
Her **early-adopter edge** shrinks to a one-year head start here.
She'd protect the **index funds** and cut rent first, a clear priority.

steps.text: Sell her AI workshop to studios while people still pay
Move with Tomas to his parents' town where rent is half
Apply to teach design in person at a local college
Post publicly asking governments to plan income support now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to be clever, maybe. Not enough to be comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people to use the five years well: learn the tools, save hard, and think about what work needs you in the room. At the studio I'd want us to agree a plan together rather than each person quietly job hunting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could ride the AI wave for three or four of those years and earn well doing it. Then around 2031 it's over for screen design. The real question is what I've built by then that isn't on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd run my workshops in person, not online, so I'm building a name as a teacher people want in the room. I'd save half of what they earn. By year three I'd want a part-time teaching post at the design college, and Tomas and I would decide by then whether to leave the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a grip on it. I know my job goes, I just get to choose the exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching? Couldn't AI teach too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could teach the facts, sure. But I've seen what nineteen-year-olds need, and a lot of it is someone telling them their work is good enough to keep going. That's people stuff, and I think colleges hold on to it longer than studios hold on to designers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ken about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's earn as much as we can from the next three years and be honest with each other about the end. Ken's in his fifties and he'll want to sell the studio before it's worth nothing. I'd rather help him do that than pretend.

say: Use the **five years well**: learn tools, save hard, find work that needs you there.
The studio should agree a **shared plan** instead of quiet job hunting.
think: She can **ride the AI wave** for three or four years and earn well.
Around **2031** screen design is over for her.
do: Run her workshops **in person** to build a name as a teacher.
Aim for a **part-time teaching** post at the design college by year three.
feel: **Anxious** but with a grip, because she chooses her exit.
S3.quote: I've seen what nineteen-year-olds need, and a lot of it is someone telling them their work is good enough to keep going.
fieldNote: She is sure her **screen job ends** but feels in control of the timing.
She bets on **in-person teaching** lasting longer than studio design.
She'd help Ken **sell the studio** rather than pretend it's fine.

steps.text: Run AI design workshops in person rather than online
Save half of everything the workshops earn
Win a part-time teaching post at the design college by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's honestly a whole other me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd keep telling designers to get good at the tools now. I'd probably still be the optimist in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the decade is mostly good years for me. AI keeps getting better and I keep being the one who uses it best at the studio, so I earn well. My job still ends in 2036, but I'd have had time to build savings, a teaching name, and maybe a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, carry on and push my workshops. Over the next few years, do a master's part-time so I can teach at a college properly, and start a family with Tomas, which we were planning anyway. Around 2032, I'd start moving out of studio work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small cloud at the edge. It's the one where I feel like myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned starting a family. Would ten years of warning change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We'd still have a baby in the next three or four years, but we'd buy smaller and closer to Tomas's parents so there's help nearby. I'd want our child to grow up with grandparents around, whatever work looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my workshop bookings dropped, that's my early warning. When studios stop paying to learn the AI tools, it means the tools don't need studios any more. I'd watch that number every month.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if people use it well.
Designers should get good at the **AI tools** now, and she'd stay the group-chat optimist.
think: The decade is mostly **good earning years** for her as the studio's AI lead.
Her job still **ends in 2036**, after time to build savings and a teaching name.
do: Do a **part-time master's** to qualify for college teaching.
Start a **family** with Tomas and buy near his parents.
Watch **workshop bookings** monthly as an early warning.
feel: **Settled**, with a small cloud at the edge.
S4.quote: When studios stop paying to learn the AI tools, it means the tools don't need studios any more. I'd watch that number every month.
fieldNote: Her income looks **safe for years**, so this sits at uneasy.
She has a clear **warning signal**: falling workshop bookings.
**Family plans** go ahead, adjusted to live near grandparents.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's degree to teach design at college
Have a baby with Tomas and buy near his parents
Keep running workshops and track bookings every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Tomas and I both lose our work in the same couple of years, and being early with the tools doesn't save either of us. What would help is some kind of income support that's agreed before it hits, and colleges hiring practitioners to teach, so people like me have somewhere to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd use it to replace other people. I already have, a bit, with Joanna's proposals. I'd like to think I'd say no to that, but if my boss Ken asked me to build the tool that replaces the junior designer, I'd probably build it.

headlineQuote: If my boss Ken asked me to build the tool that replaces the junior designer, I'd probably build it.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old brand designer** who runs the AI workflow at a five-person startup-branding studio.
She has a **year of savings** and index funds, and lives with Tomas, a software tester.
She stays **calm or uneasy** while a person is needed to run the tools, and alarmed when not.
Her chosen exit is **in-person teaching**, through workshops now and a part-time master's later.
She's honest that her tool demos have already **squeezed a colleague's** job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Tomas would both lose their screen-based work at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** agreed before the change hits.
